replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Putting the fees in and then logging live dry-run trades is the right order, since live data shows fills that a backtest only assumes. When you compare, look at how far the live entries and exits land from the backtest ones, because that gap is what usually eats the edge. A win rate that high often means the losses are rare but large, so I'd watch the worst single loss and the drawdown more than the win rate. A couple of weeks of live logging across different market conditions will tell you more than the longer backtest.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
running it dry on a server before real money is exactly the right last step, most people skip it. two things that saved me some pain at this stage:

write down now what result over the dry run counts as "go", like minimum average R per trade after fees, max drawdown, and minimum number of trades. once results come in it's really easy to move the bar.

and check how the dry mode fills orders. a lot of paper engines fill a limit order the moment price touches it, but in reality you only get filled when price trades through your level, and on 5m SOL that difference alone can eat a small TP. if your log stores the touch price and the next trade price, you'll see how big the gap is.

one more thing on 13 days of XRP at 100%: trades on the same days move together, so that's closer to a handful of real data points. let it run a couple of months across up, down and sideways weeks and then it'll tell you something.

if you're up for it, DM me the dry-run log once you've got a month or so, happy to go through it with you.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
logging that much from day one is great, most people only find out what they should have logged after it breaks.

one thing to double check with bar-close triggers: in the backtest, does the entry fill at that same bar's close? in live you can only act after the bar has closed, so the real fill is the next tick or the next bar's open. on 5m bars that small gap is often a big chunk of a 0.35% minimum trade. if the dry run logs the signal bar close next to the actual fill price, you'll see it right away.

and I get the "not working isn't an option" feeling, I had it too. what helped me was the opposite: writing down beforehand what result would mean it doesn't work, so if the dry run says no, it's a clear answer and not months of tweaking. the rules you'd trust live are usually the ones that survived a test you were ready to fail.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
one thing worth running the numbers on before going live: at 25x, a 2.3% stop is roughly 57% of the margin on that position, and liquidation sits around 3.5-4% away depending on the exchange's maintenance margin. so there's less than 2% between your stop and liquidation, and on SOL a fast wick or slippage on the stop can jump that gap.

what usually works better: size each trade by risk instead of by leverage. decide you lose, say, 1% of the account if the stop hits, and the position size follows from the stop distance. leverage then just becomes whatever is needed to hold that size, usually way less than 25x. same expected return per trade, much less chance one bad candle ends the account.

the 1.33% biggest loss over 30 days is a good sign, but 30 days won't include the worst candle you'll see. that's the one the sizing has to survive.
